extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), respondents in USPTO disciplinary proceedings, and USPTO enforcement staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in an Administrative Law Judge's decision finding professional misconduct by a USPTO practitioner and determining appropriate sanctions (exclusion/suspension). Covers rule violations, duties to clients/public/profession, sanctioning factors, and related procedural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (pre-May-3-2013 Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where Respondent filed an application even though he knew, or should have known, that a patent was statutorily barred pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 102(b). The decision treats filing a statutorily barred patent application as conduct proscribed by this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (pre-May-3-2013 Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where Respondent submitted an application he knew or should have known was statutorily barred; such submission is considered prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a) & (b) via 10.23(c)(15) — signing papers in violation of § 11.18 / reasonable inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes signing a paper filed in the Office in violation of the provisions of § 11.18, which requires practitioners to conduct a reasonable inquiry and certify that legal contentions are warranted by existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent signed a Utility Patent Application Transmittal when he knew, or failed to conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances to determine, that the patent was statutorily barred. Rule requires reasonable inquiry before certifying papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(b) — handling a legal matter without adequate preparation (pre-May-3-2013 Code)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes handling a legal matter without preparation adequate in the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing an application when the practitioner knew or should have known it was statutorily barred constitutes inadequate preparation under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h)(1) — public discipline by state authority as professional misconduct (post-May-3-2013 Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to be publicly disciplined on ethical or professional misconduct grounds by any duly constituted authority of a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treats a public reprimand by the New Jersey Supreme Court (adopting the Disciplinary Review Board decision) as establishing a violation of this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(a)(1) — duty to withdraw when representation will result in a rule violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes failing to withdraw from the representation of a client when the representation will result in a violation of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent failed to withdraw from trademark matters while ineligible to practice before the Office, violating this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.505 — engaging in the unauthorized practice of law (post-May-3-2013 Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in the unauthorized practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied where Respondent represented others before the Office in trademark matters from August 25, 2014 through October 16, 2015 while ineligible to practice law in any state.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (post-May-3-2013 Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent falsely represented himself to clients and to the Office as authorized to practice in trademark matters when he was ineligible; such conduct violates § 11.804(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (post-May-3-2013 Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's false representations to the Office about his authorization to practice in trademark matters are treated as prejudicial under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.14 — authorization to practice before the Office depends on state licensure / good standing
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who is not a member in good standing of the highest court of a state is not authorized to practice before the USPTO in trademark matters (and is otherwise ineligible under the rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent was administratively ineligible to practice law in New Jersey and therefore was not authorized to practice before the Office in trademark matters during the period cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 — certification of papers; requirement to conduct a reasonable inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires practitioners to conduct a reasonable inquiry and certify that the legal contentions contained in a paper filed in the Office are warranted by existing law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing a Utility Patent Application Transmittal without conducting a reasonable inquiry (when claims were statutorily barred) violates § 11.18; §11.18 underpins several of the cited misconduct rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)) — four-factor framework for imposing sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider: (1) whether a duty was violated (to client, public, legal system, or profession); (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies these four factors to conclude exclusion is appropriate: (1) finds duty violations to clients and the patent bar; (2) finds Respondent acted knowingly and intentionally; (3) finds significant potential injury though no proffered actual injuries; (4) identifies multiple aggravating factors supporting a severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA Standards and case law examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding (e.g., intentionally failing to respond to Court orders), a pattern of multiple violations, and substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court cites the ABA Standards and prior USPTO disciplinary decisions, and finds aggravating factors here: failure to respond (obstruction), multiple counts/pattern of misconduct over more than a year, and Respondent's 38+ years of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors — consideration in sanctioning (absence here)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court must consider any mitigating factors that might lessen sanction severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notes no mitigating factors were found to offset the aggravating factors; absence of mitigation contributes to imposition of exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to clients and the profession — fiduciary/communication duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners owe fiduciary duties to clients (e.g., to communicate material information and act competently) and duties to the profession/public to maintain integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent violated duties by failing to conduct reasonable inquiry as to statutory bar, not informing Ms. Nagy of an Office Action, and falsely holding himself out as authorized to practice; such breaches weigh heavily in sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate with clients — inform clients of material developments
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must communicate with clients about material developments in matters they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to inform Ms. Nagy of the Non-Final Office Action rejecting claims and of the bar to patentability was cited as professional misconduct by the New Jersey disciplinary authorities and by the Court here.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.55(a) — right to appeal an initial decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party may file an appeal to the USPTO Director within thirty (30) days of an initial decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural notice provided to Respondent; an appeal is the avenue to challenge the sanction and findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 — practitioner responsibilities during suspension or exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifies practitioner responsibilities in cases of suspension or exclusion (notice to clients, files, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent is directed to § 11.58 regarding obligations following exclusion; the rule governs what excluded practitioners must do.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.60 — petition for reinstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Governs the right and procedure for a practitioner to petition for reinstatement after suspension or exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision provides notice of the right to petition for reinstatement under § 11.60 as the post-sanction remedial route.
